title: Roadmap
text:
Next

Policy simulator v2.0. Rebuild the Pull the Right Lever simulator on the v2.0 model, with the girls/boys groups and the new intake terms as levers.
Adding a new year. When DfE publishes a new year’s KS4 results, add it to YEAR_CONFIG in pipeline/helpers.R, run R/00_fetch_data.R, then the build steps. The v2.0 model takes its years from the data, and no longer needs the workforce file, which was the slowest to arrive. See the README.
A self-contained data pipeline for the model. R/00_fetch_data.R builds every model input from public sources (DfE, GIAS, ONS, nomis, postcodes.io, Ofsted), with the scripts in pipeline/. Rebuilt from the same downloads it reproduces the inputs, and every value-added figure, exactly.
The Sussex area analyses, self-contained too. The area pages still reuse the original project’s area analyses (a snapshot in data/area/), its Sussex governance and its absence reasons. Port its R/15, R/17 and R/19 next.
Update 2025/26 with the revised KS4 release (February 2027). 2025/26 is shown now, provisional, predicted from the fitted model on DfE’s October results with absence bridged and the unpublished intake data carried forward (R/05_provisional_2526.R). Rerun it on the revised results; then, once the year’s census, SEN and mobility data are out, fold 2025/26 into the model as a fifth year.
v2.1 candidates: the kind of absence, and 11–16 schools. The illness share of absence and an 11–16 flag both improve the model’s fit; see Brighton and Hove’s authority effect. Test them across every group before adopting either, and look at a parents’ qualification measure from the 2021 Census in place of neighbourhood education for all adults.
Areas beyond Sussex. The area template works for any authority and its districts once boundaries are added.
Monthly Ofsted refresh. A GitHub Actions workflow picks up Ofsted’s new release on the 20th of each month, updates every school’s latest judgement without refitting, rerenders and commits.
Publish v2.0 alongside v1 in the original reports, labelled, with a note on how rankings change.

title: Brighton and Hove’s authority effect
text:
NoteIn short



On the v2.0 model Brighton and Hove has the 4th largest local authority effect of 152: its schools’ Attainment 8 runs +3.8% above what intake and context predict, after neighbourhood education is taken into account. Almost all of it is an absence effect. The city’s absence is among the highest in England, the model expects that absence to cost attainment, and in Brighton and Hove it costs much less than expected. Take absence out of the model and the authority falls to 60th. The extra absence is mostly authorised illness. Why it costs so little here is the open question, and family-level resources are one of the likely answers.



How large, and how steady
The effect is there for every group of pupils and in every year:

A school in Brighton and Hove averages +0.7 to +2.5 points a year above similar schools in England. That is not one good cohort.


It is an absence effect

Without absence the effect falls from +3.8% to +0.8%, indistinguishable from zero.
Without neighbourhood education or without prior attainment it grows, to +5.6% and +6.9%. Both are already working: the city’s intakes are more advantaged on both, and the model credits that. See neighbourhood education below.
Local segregation changes nothing. Brighton and Hove’s catchment admissions, with random allocation as a tie-break, keep its schools relatively mixed, but that does not explain the effect.
An 11–16 flag takes a little off. 60% of Brighton and Hove’s school-years are at 11–16 schools, against 37% in England. Nationally, 11–16 schools score +1.0% higher.

The arithmetic. Over 2021/22 to 2024/25, the four years the model is fitted on, Brighton and Hove’s schools average 10.9% full-year absence against 9.0% for England (means of school-years), 6th highest of 152 authorities. In 2024/25 alone, the year the area page’s add-and-take figure uses, it was 11.3% against 8.6% (means of schools): the gap has widened. On the v2.0 absence coefficient (-0.226, an elasticity), that difference lowers expected Attainment 8 by 4.5%. The authority effect, +3.8%, almost exactly gives it back. Brighton and Hove’s schools attain about what similar intakes attain elsewhere. They do it despite absence that, elsewhere, goes with lower results.
Inside the city, absence costs about what it costs elsewhere. A school with more absence than its neighbours does worse by about the national rate: the interaction is +0.033 (standard error 0.042). It is the city’s level of absence that carries no penalty, not its slope.

Of Brighton and Hove’s 1.9 points of extra absence, 1.4 is authorised illness. Unauthorised absence is close to England’s. Illness makes up 57% of absence in the city (36th highest share of 152).
Nationally, illness absence costs less than other absence. Split in two, a 1% rise in illness absence goes with -0.06% Attainment 8 and a 1% rise in other absence with -0.12%. Allowing for that takes some of the effect away: to +3.6% with the illness share, +2.7% with absence split. It does not take most of it away. Absence’s type, as DfE records it, is part of the story, not the whole of it.


Neighbourhood education
v2.0 measures neighbourhood education as the share of adults with a degree-level (level 4+) qualification in the 150 Census output areas nearest each school, from the 2021 Census. It is there because a school’s results follow the education of the families around it, and FSM sees only the bottom of that.
Where the city’s schools sit. Their neighbourhoods average 43.4% of adults at level 4+, against 33.2% around England’s schools: about 1.0 standard deviation higher, 25th of 152 authorities. The share with no qualifications is 13.9% against 18.8%. 9 of the city’s 10 schools sit above England’s median school:

What the model already credits. Each standard deviation of neighbourhood education is worth +2.40% of Attainment 8 for all pupils, +2.54% for non-disadvantaged pupils and only +0.78% for disadvantaged ones. Set against England, the city’s neighbourhoods lift its schools’ expected Attainment 8 by about +1.1 points for all pupils, +1.3 for non-disadvantaged and +0.3 for disadvantaged pupils. That is credit the schools do not get: it is in the expectation, not in their value added.
Without the term, the authority effect would be +5.7% (3rd) rather than +3.9%. Neighbourhood education already accounts for about 31% of what would otherwise look like a city effect.
Would a better measure take more? The table refits the model with the neighbourhood drawn at every scale the original project built, and with the share of adults with no qualifications:

No. A more local neighbourhood fits worse at every step, and leaves the city’s effect larger: +4.8% with the 5 nearest output areas. The no-qualifications share fits worse than level 4+. The best fit, level 4+ and no qualifications, 150 nearest, moves the effect only to +3.7%. Neighbourhood education is doing what it can, and the rest is not a neighbourhood the Census can see.
What it cannot see. The measure counts every adult, not parents. Brighton and Hove has two universities: students, whose highest qualification while studying is usually level 3, and young graduates without school-age children both sit in the count, in opposite directions, and neither says much about the families whose children attend the schools. A measure of parents’ qualifications, from the Census tables for households with dependent children, would test this directly (reading 1 below).


So what is it?
The data are school-level, so they cannot settle this. Four readings fit what is above, and they are not exclusive.

Family resources that keep learning going. A day off costs less when someone at home can help catch up: parents with degrees, flexible or home-based work, tutoring, books. FSM does not see this, and neither, quite, does neighbourhood education, which already takes about 31% of the effect and can take no more however it is drawn (above). It counts every adult, not parents. The effect is largest for boys and non-disadvantaged pupils (3rd of 151–152 for both). It is also present for disadvantaged pupils (16th), which fits a city with many lower-income households that are highly educated.
Absence as a stand-in. Across England, high absence travels with things the model does not measure: family stress, poverty beyond FSM, disengagement. Part of the absence coefficient is those things, not the days missed. Where absence comes from somewhere else, the model over-predicts its cost. In Brighton and Hove it is mostly authorised illness, which may include anxiety and other health-related absence that follows a different pattern from disengagement. On this reading the authority effect is partly an artefact of how v2.0 treats absence, not something the schools do.
Recording. Schools and authorities differ in when they authorise illness and how they code it. A practice that authorises more parent-reported illness raises recorded absence without changing learning. This would show up as exactly this pattern, and school-level data cannot tell it from reading 2.
Something the schools or the system do. The 11–16 structure, where entry to the city’s sixth-form colleges depends on GCSE grades, explains a little. Mixed intakes explain nothing measurable. Whatever is left after absence (+0.8%, ranked 60th) is ordinary.



What would help tell them apart
All of these are published:

Absence by pupil characteristics, by authority (DfE, Pupil absence in schools in England). Is the city’s extra absence among pupils eligible for free school meals or not, and in which year groups? Reading 1 predicts it is mostly among the non-disadvantaged.
Census 2021 qualifications for parents rather than all adults: households with dependent children by the household reference person’s qualification or NS-SeC, for school neighbourhoods. This would test reading 1 directly, and would improve v2.0’s neighbourhood term everywhere students and young graduates are concentrated.
Persistent absence and absence reasons by authority over time, against attainment. Reading 3 predicts the city’s illness authorisation sits apart from its neighbours’ with no matching change in attainment.
Elective home education and children missing education (DfE, by authority). These show whether pupils leave school rolls before Year 11 at unusual rates, which would change who sits GCSEs.
Attainment by prior-attainment band in the KS4 performance tables: whether the effect sits with high, middle or low prior attainers.



What it means for v2.0
v2.0 treats a day of absence the same whatever its cause. Adding the illness share of absence improves the model’s fit (AIC -30) and barely changes other authorities’ effects (correlation 0.997). It is a candidate for a v2.1, with the 11–16 flag (-33). Neither removes Brighton and Hove’s effect. Until the questions above are answered, read the city’s authority effect this way: its schools achieve as much as similar schools elsewhere despite unusually high, mostly illness, absence. It is not evidence that the city’s schools add more than others. With no allowance for absence, the city’s schools average -0.5 points of value added, 95th of 151 authorities.
The models are in R/06_bh_effect.R.

title: How much does a school add? And how much does absence (or anything else) take away?
text: Value Added v2.0 measures each secondary school in England against what its intake and context would lead us to expect: for all pupils, for disadvantaged and non-disadvantaged pupils, and now for girls and boys. It is the next step from How to Pull the Right Lever, rebuilt on the recommendations of a review of the original measure.

title: How much does a school add? And how much does absence (or anything else) take away?
section: What a school adds, and what absence takes away
text:
What a school adds, and what absence takes away
Value added measures what a school does after its intake and context are accounted for, absence included. So the two quantities below are not the same thing counted twice: one is what absence moves, the other is what the school moves once absence has already been allowed for.








Figure 1: An average school, then the same school with absence where the highest 5% of schools sit (full-year absence in 2024/25, 13.0% against a median of 8.4%), then that school doing everything a school can do (value added 2021/22 to 2024/25). Blue is what absence takes away, purple what the school adds back. Attainment 8 points; the dashed line is the England average of 47.5.





Read it left to right. An average school sits at the England mean. Put its absence where the highest 5% of schools sit (13.0% full-year absence in 2024/25, against a typical 8.4%) and it loses 4.6 Attainment 8 points. Now ask it to do everything a school can do – to be a top-ten-per-cent school on value added, net of its intake – and it gains 3.2 back. It is still 1.3 points below where it started. Being exceptional buys back about 71% of what high absence costs.
It also falls hardest on the pupils with the least room to absorb it. The same change in absence is worth 5.1 points of disadvantaged pupils’ Attainment 8, against 4.6 for pupils as a whole, and from a lower base: it takes 13.3% of what they would otherwise score rather than 9.6%, a gradient 41% steeper. Absence is not only the largest lever, it is a regressive one.
One caveat, stated plainly because the scale of this invites over-reading. The model is associational. The gradient says what schools with more absence look like once intake is accounted for, not what a particular school would gain by cutting absence by a given amount. The direction and the order of magnitude are what to take from it. How each number is computed from the model is set out in the methodology.

title: How much does a school add? And how much does absence (or anything else) take away?
text:
What is new in v2.0

Measured against intake and context only. The Ofsted grade and the teacher workforce terms are out of the expectation: they partly reflect the very performance being measured.
Fairer to schools with harder intakes. Pupil mobility, SEN rates, a single-sex term and neighbourhood education are in.
Against England. A school is compared with similar schools anywhere, with the local authority’s own effect reported beside it.
Honest about uncertainty. Estimates are shrunk by their reliability and carry 95% intervals.
Girls and boys have their own value added for the first time.
The latest Ofsted judgement sits beside every school, including the new report cards.
Over time. Every school has a figure for each year, so trajectories and moving averages over a chosen window sit beside the four-year figure.

title: Methodology – Value Added v2.0
text:
NoteIn one line



Value added v2.0 is each school’s Attainment 8 above or below what a multilevel model expects from its intake and context, measured against England, for five groups of pupils, 2021/22 to 2024/25.

title: Methodology – Value Added v2.0
section: What is Bayesian here, and what is not
text:
What is Bayesian here, and what is not
\(\lambda\bar r\) is exactly the posterior mean of a school’s effect under a normal prior centred on zero with variance \(\tau^2\). The arithmetic is Bayesian; the prior is not chosen. \(\tau^2\) and \(\sigma^2\) are estimated by REML from the same data the shrinkage is then applied to, which makes this empirical Bayes rather than Bayes. There is no hyperprior, no sampling and nothing to converge: the posterior is Gaussian and closed form.
The price is that the intervals treat \(\tau^2\) and \(\sigma^2\) as known. They carry the uncertainty in a school’s own mean, not the uncertainty in the variances used to shrink it, so they are a little tighter than a fully Bayesian treatment would give — most so for the groups with the fewest schools.

title: Methodology – Value Added v2.0
section: Two variances, because there are two questions
text:
Two variances, because there are two questions
Against England, a school is credited with everything that separates it from the national picture, its authority and its region included. The prior variance for that comparison is therefore all three persistent components together:
\[\tau^2_\text{England} = \tau^2_\text{school} + \tau^2_\text{LA} + \tau^2_\text{region}\]
Within the authority, the authority and region effects are already in the prediction and are not the school’s to own, so the prior variance is the school component alone. The national figure is the less shrunk of the two: there is more real variation there for it to be variation of. For all pupils that is \(\tau_\text{England} =
0.064\) against \(\tau_\text{school} = 0.059\) on the log scale.

title: Methodology – Value Added v2.0
text:
Back to Attainment 8 points
Shrinkage happens on the log scale, where the model is additive. The shrunken effect is converted against the school’s own mean expected Attainment 8:
\[\text{value added} = \text{base}\left(e^{\lambda\bar r} - 1\right)\]
and its 95% interval the same way, from \(\lambda\bar r \pm
1.96\sqrt{\lambda\sigma^2/n}\). A school counts as significant where that interval excludes zero.
This is a different quantity from the plain four-year mean sitting beside it in the tables: that one averages observed minus expected in points, while this one shrinks a mean log residual and then converts it. For most schools the two are close. For schools with short records or unusual intakes they are not, and the shrunken figure is the one to read.

title: The Value-Added Review
text:
WarningWhere this led



Every recommendation below has been adopted in Value Added v2.0. This page is the review as written, with its figures recomputed from the same analysis (R/21_value_added_review.R in the original repository).
A review of the value-added measure used across the How to Pull the Right Lever work and the Sussex documents. Every figure comes from refitting the published national model on its own data, 12,195 school-years for 3,300 schools, 2021/22 to 2024/25. Nothing uses pupil-level records.

title: The Value-Added Review
section: Why a drop in AIC, and not a Shapley decomposition
text:
Why a drop in AIC, and not a Shapley decomposition
The original lever work decomposed Attainment 8 with Shapley values – the LMG decomposition, which averages each term’s contribution over every order in which the terms could have entered. The table above looks like the same exercise. It is not, and the difference changes how the table should be read.
Dropping a term from the full model measures what that term explains that nothing else does. It is the “added last” extreme: a term is credited with none of the variation it shares with its neighbours. Shapley averages over all orders of entry, so each term is credited with the shared variation exactly as often as it is denied it. The two agree only when the terms are uncorrelated, and these terms are emphatically not: prior attainment, absence and disadvantage all describe overlapping things about the same intake.
The clearest evidence is in the table itself. Disadvantage comes fifth on AIC, below both the Ofsted grade and the local authority, which reads as though how poor a school’s intake is matters less to attainment than its inspection grade. It does not. It means that with prior attainment and absence already in the model there is little left for disadvantage to explain on its own – those two have absorbed most of it. A Shapley decomposition would hand that shared variation back and disadvantage would rise sharply. The bullet above is the same point stated as a finding; it is better understood as a property of the measure.
So the two answer different questions, and neither is the better tool in general:

A drop in AIC asks whether a term earns its place in the model. That is a specification question, and it is the one this document is asking. The penalty means a term has to buy its parameter, and a term that cannot – segregation here – is one the published measure should not be carrying.
A Shapley decomposition asks how to divide the credit between terms that are already in. That is an attribution question, and it was the right one for the lever work, which had to say how much of a gap each driver accounted for. It is also far more expensive: every subset of the terms has to be fitted, against one refit per term here.

Read the table, then, as what it is: how much each term carries that no other term does, beside how far the answer moves without it. For practical purposes the second column is the one to lean on, because it says how many schools actually change quintile rather than how much likelihood is lost. Neither column is a statement about how much each thing matters to a child’s results, and the AIC column in particular should not be quoted as a ranking of importance.

title: The Value-Added Review
section: Things schools partly control: workforce and Ofsted
text:
Things schools partly control: workforce and Ofsted
The workforce terms. Retention, leadership pay and sickness absence are shaped by a school’s leadership as well as by its circumstances. In the baseline, a school that keeps its teachers is expected to do better, so the credit for doing so is netted off its value added. Dropping all three moves 19% of schools a quintile for all pupils, nearly all of it retention, and 7% for disadvantaged pupils. The fit loss is small (AIC 168).
The Ofsted grade. This is the more serious problem. Ofsted’s judgements draw on a school’s results, so putting the grade in the expectation partly conditions value added on its own outcome. An Outstanding school’s bar is raised (the grade’s random effect has a standard deviation of 4.2%), and some of its added value disappears into it. Removing the grade:

moves 34% of schools a quintile (26% for disadvantaged pupils);
changes value added by 0.7 points on average, and by more than 1.6 for one school in ten;
raises the fixed effects’ share of variance (marginal R² from 0.65 to 0.71), because the intake terms take back what the grade had absorbed.

The grade was useful for the Lever report’s purpose, which was to explain attainment. It is the wrong thing to hold constant when the aim is to measure a school against its intake.

title: The Value-Added Review
section: Intake the model misses: mobility, gender, SEN
text:
Intake the model misses: mobility, gender, SEN

Mobility is the best single addition: AIC -293 for all pupils and -241 for disadvantaged. Each extra percentage point of mobile pupils costs 0.5% of Attainment 8. It moves 15% of schools.
Gender. A girls’ school scores +5.4% above an otherwise identical mixed school (boys’ schools do not differ, at -0.1%). A single-sex flag (AIC -191) fits better than the share of girls as a continuous term (AIC -178): the effect is a girls’-school effect, not a gradient across mixed schools.
SEN. SEN support and EHCP rates improve the fit modestly for all pupils (AIC -99) and more clearly for disadvantaged pupils (-93), and move few schools. They belong in the expectation on principle: a school’s SEN intake is not of its making.

title: The Value-Added Review
text:
Neighbourhood education
The preliminary work (Analysis F in the model experiments) found that the share of adults with degree-level qualifications in the 150 census output areas nearest a school, about a 2.5 km radius, improved the model and explained part of the local authority effect. In this review’s terms:

For all pupils it is a strong addition: AIC -239, and one standard deviation of neighbourhood education is worth +2.2%. The local authority standard deviation falls from 0.0262 to 0.0219: it accounts for 30% of the authority variance. Brighton and Hove’s effect falls from +4.5% (5th) to +2.9% (10th). Part of what looked like a Brighton and Hove effect is the city’s educated neighbourhoods.
For disadvantaged pupils it does nothing (AIC +1.4, effect +0.1%). Brighton and Hove’s rank barely moves, from 14th to 15th. Living near educated households does not raise disadvantaged pupils’ results; it is non-disadvantaged pupils, many of whose parents are those households, who carry the effect.

That pattern is what one would expect if neighbourhood education stands in for parental education, which no school-level source measures directly. On that reading it is intake, and belongs in the expectation. Two cautions:

it describes the area around the school, not where its pupils live, so schools with wide or unusual catchments are measured imperfectly;
it is fixed at the 2021 Census, so it cannot track change.


How the neighbourhood is drawn, and why 150
This is the part of v2.0 with no counterpart in the published measure, so it is worth setting out plainly rather than leaving in a citation.
For each school we take its coordinates from GIAS, find the 150 nearest 2021 Census Output Area population-weighted centroids – an exact kd-tree search on the British National Grid, so the distances are metres on the ground and not degrees – and average the census indicators over those output areas. An output area holds about 125 households, so 150 of them is on the order of nineteen thousand: a slice of a town, rather than a street or a region. The indicator the model carries is the share of adults qualified to level 4 or above. Unemployment and economic inactivity were built the same way and are strongly collinear with it, which is why only one of the three is in the specification.
150 was not picked for roundness. The preliminary work built the same variables at k = 10, 25, 50, 100 and 150 and let the fit choose. AIC falls steadily as k grows, bottoms out around 150, and then plateaus and slightly reverses. That shape matters: a variable drifting toward a regional average would keep on improving the fit as the window widened, so a genuine minimum is evidence that 150 is picking up something local rather than washing out into region. Primary schools, run the same way in earlier work, prefer k = 10.
That contrast is the real finding. k is a scale parameter, and the fit recovers catchment geography from the data: secondaries draw from much further than primaries, and the model knows it without being told. At k = 150 the mean radius is about 2.5 km.
There is also a falsification check, which is what makes this more than curve fitting. If the term captures the neighbourhood a school actually serves, rather than generic regional conditions, it should be weaker for schools with a religious character, whose admission is less distance-based by construction. The interaction carries the predicted negative sign, but is not conventionally significant: directionally supportive, underpowered.








Figure 4: One school’s neighbourhood: Dorothy Stringer School (pink) and the 150 nearest 2021 Census output-area population-weighted centroids (purple), with the extent they cover shaded. These are the output areas the neighbourhood term averages over. Hover a centroid for its distance from the school.




For this school the 150th output area is 1.7 km away and the mean is 1.1 km – a compact, genuinely local patch. The same 150 output areas around a rural school would sprawl much further, which is the honest limitation of a fixed k: it is a constant number of households, not a constant distance, so it adapts to population density rather than to how far a particular school’s pupils travel.

title: The Value-Added Review
section: Who runs the school: route and trusts
text:
Who runs the school: route and trusts
Converter academies score +0.9% against maintained schools, free schools, UTCs and studio schools -2.2%, and sponsor-led academies +0.2%. Schools in a multi-academy trust score +1.1%. None of this moves value added much (correlations 0.99 and 1.00).
More importantly, governance should not be in the expectation at all. Who runs a school is one of the things value added is meant to reveal: a trust that improves its schools should see that in their value added, not have it netted off. The worry about selection, that trusts take on schools in difficult circumstances, is met by measuring those circumstances directly (disadvantage, prior attainment, mobility, SEN), not by adjusting for governance. The trust analysis in the East Sussex document is the right place for the governance question.

title: The Value-Added Review
text:
Size and religious character
School size improves the fit for all pupils (AIC -99) but should stay out: popular, successful schools grow, so size is partly a consequence of value added. Religious character makes no difference (AIC +1.9).

title: The Value-Added Review
text:
Absence
Absence is the model’s second most important term. Dropping it moves 45% of schools a quintile, and Brighton and Hove’s authority effect from 5th in England to 30th. It is partly intake (illness, deprivation) and partly practice. The Lever report’s argument rests on keeping it in, and the joint-signal plane already shows the other view, value added with attendance counted in. That pairing is the right answer and needs no change: keep absence in the core measure, and keep publishing the attendance-counted-in version beside it.

title: The Value-Added Review
section: Against the authority, or against England
text:
Against the authority, or against England
The published value added includes the local authority’s random effect in the expectation. With ten or twenty schools in an authority, that effect is largely the average of those schools’ own results, so part of each school’s added value is attributed to its authority and netted off. Measuring against England instead (leaving the authority and region effects out of the prediction):

correlates 0.91 with the published value added across schools, and moves 41% of schools a quintile (42% for disadvantaged pupils);
shifts every school in an authority by the same amount, so it changes comparisons between authorities, not within them.









Figure 5: Each school’s published value added (within its local authority) against its value added measured against England, all pupils, mean 2021/22 to 2024/25. Sussex schools coloured by authority.





Both views are legitimate, but they answer different questions:

Within the authority: “how does this school do compared with similar schools in the same place?”
Against England: “how does this school do compared with similar schools anywhere?”

For the Sussex documents, which compare schools across three authorities, the national version is the right one, and the authority effect should be reported beside it rather than inside it.

title: The Value-Added Review
section: How much of value added is the school
text:
How much of value added is the school
A version of the published model with a school random intercept splits the unexplained variation into a persistent school part and year-to-year noise:

All pupils: the school part has a standard deviation of 0.074 (log scale) against 0.057 for the year-to-year noise. 63% of the unexplained variation is persistent. A four-year average has a reliability of 0.85.
Disadvantaged pupils: 37% persistent, and a four-year average reliability of 0.67. The groups are small, and single years are noisy.

The shrunken school effects from that model correlate 0.90 with the averaged residuals for all pupils, and 0.96 for disadvantaged pupils. The simple average is a good approximation. The shrunken estimate is better for small schools and should be preferred where single schools are singled out.
